patient.chief_complaint: Progressive headaches, new left arm weakness, and a first-time seizure
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Dalton is a 58-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His wife reports that over the past three weeks, he has been complaining of progressively worsening headaches, predominantly on the right side, which are worst in the early morning and occasionally wake him from sleep. He has been using over-the-counter ibuprofen with only marginal relief. She also noticed that about two weeks ago, he began having difficulty using his left hand at work, dropping tools and struggling with fine motor tasks such as buttoning his shirt. She describes him as being somewhat more forgetful and 'not himself' over the past ten days, occasionally repeating questions and seeming confused about appointments. This morning at approximately 07:15, while eating breakfast, his wife observed his left arm begin to shake rhythmically, followed within thirty seconds by his eyes rolling back and a generalized convulsion lasting approximately ninety seconds. He was postictal and confused for about fifteen minutes afterward. EMS was called and he was transported to the emergency department. On arrival, he was alert and conversant but had a persistent mild headache. He denies any prior seizure history, recent head trauma, febrile illness, vision changes, nausea, or vomiting. He has not had any recent weight loss or night sweats. His wife reports no recent travel or sick contacts. A non-contrast CT scan obtained in the emergency department revealed a large hyperdense mass in the right frontal lobe with surrounding hypodensity consistent with edema and approximately 7 mm of midline shift to the left. He was admitted to the neurology service for further workup.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with significant midline shift (8 mm): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Administer dexamethasone (loading dose 10 mg IV, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema and mass effect (8 mm midline shift)
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
Monitor blood glucose closely given anticipated corticosteroid use in a patient with diabetes; adjust antihyperglycemic regimen as needed
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of mass effect (8 mm midline shift) — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right frontal heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Significant midline shift / herniation risk mandates urgent dexamethasone and neurosurgical evaluation; lumbar puncture is contraindicated
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)
